changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For ecommerce buyers losing high-value orders at checkout: "Stop your big orders dying at the last step. We'll show you why your large baskets get declined, what those failed orders are worth, and what we change to win them back." Keep the average uplift (Authorization Boost / Adaptive Acceptance) only as supporting proof under this line, never as the headline value claim.
changes.why: The customer's pain was one in twelve orders failing, worst on big baskets, with no explanation from the processor, and she described it as 'orders dying at the last step'; our average-uplift slide was what we leaned on, and it did not carry the case.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: For the CFO or finance approver, especially when they won't meet us and the champion has to carry the case: "Your ROI in your numbers: we run your own decline export and put the value of your failed orders next to your total payment cost, on one page you can hand your CFO." Make this one-pager the standard answer to 'something I can hand my CFO' instead of the deck and pricing proposal.
changes.why: Lucy asked for something to hand Martin and got the deck and the pricing proposal. We skipped Farah's offer to analyse their declines, so the CFO decided on a rate-only page and saw 'the same thing'.

changes.change: Counter line for when an incumbent bank or processor sharpens its rate: "A better rate on the same failed orders is still losing you orders. Here's what your declines cost next to the rate difference." Use it to pull the conversation back from rate to the cost of declines before the customer's finance team builds a rate-against-rate comparison.
changes.why: When the bank cut its rate, the conversation moved from declines to 'can you do better on the rate', and the deal was decided on a side-by-side rate page. We had no line to bring it back to the failed orders.
